[1] In our family the bakery was not a place but a time. It opened at ten at night, when the rest of Calder Street was pulling its shutters down, and it closed at six in the morning, when the first buses began to sigh at the corner. For the first eleven years of my life I knew it mainly as a set of sounds coming up through the floor of the apartment: the mixer starting with a cough, the oven doors, my father's radio turned low to a station that played nothing but old ballads and weather.

[2] My brother Nico had been allowed downstairs at twelve. My sister Rosa had been allowed at twelve too. I was the youngest, and so I was the one who was always being sent back up the stairs with a roll in a paper napkin, as if a roll were the same thing as being there.

[3] The night I finally went down to stay, I had imagined it so often that the real room surprised me by being small. The bench in the middle was floured like a field after the first snow, and my mother stood at one end of it, cutting dough into pieces on a scale without seeming to look at the scale. My father nodded at me the way he nodded at a delivery driver. Rosa handed me an apron that had been hers, and then Nico's, and that still had his initials inked inside the collar.

[4] "Don't touch anything warm," Nico said. "Don't touch anything cold either, actually. Just watch."

[5] I watched for about an hour. What I had pictured as a kind of magic turned out to be mostly waiting. The dough was mixed and then it rested; it was shaped and then it rested; it went into the cool cabinet my parents called the retarder, and then it rested there for hours. My father checked it by pressing one finger into a loaf and watching how the dent came back. "Comes back fast, it's not ready," he said, mostly to the dough. "Doesn't come back at all, you've waited too long. You want it to come back slow, like it's thinking about it."

[6] At two o'clock my mother gave me a job. It was the plainest job in the room, brushing egg wash onto the braided loaves before they went in, and she showed me once and went back to her scale. I did the first tray with such care that by the time I finished, the loaves at the start had begun to dry. Rosa looked over my shoulder and said nothing, which was worse than if she had said something.

[7] The second tray I did faster. The third I did faster still, and somewhere in the middle of it I stopped thinking about my hands. I noticed instead that the radio had moved from ballads to the marine forecast, and that my father hummed along with the names of the coastal stations as if they were a song he had always known. I noticed that my mother, at the scale, was saying numbers under her breath, and that Nico, at the ovens, was saying the same numbers back a few seconds later. They were not talking to each other. They were keeping time.

[8] Around four, I made my mistake. I lifted a tray off the rack too quickly and one braid slid off and folded against the edge of the bench. I stood holding the tray, waiting for someone to say my name in the voice that meant I would be going back upstairs. My father came over, looked at the loaf, and pressed his finger into it. The dent came back slowly.

[9] "This one we sell to ourselves," he said, and set it on the shelf where the family's bread went, the ones that would never sit in the window. Then he went back to the oven. That was all.

[10] At six o'clock Rosa turned the sign on the door. The first customer was a bus driver who bought two rolls and did not look at any of us, and I felt, absurdly, insulted on behalf of the whole night, all those hours folded into a thing he would eat in four bites at a red light. I said so to Nico on the stairs. He shrugged. "That's the point," he said. "He's not supposed to know."

[11] We ate the folded braid at breakfast. It was a little lopsided and perfectly good, and my father cut the first slice and handed it to me without a word, the way he would hand you a tool.
prompt: According to paragraph 5, the narrator's father judged whether the dough was ready by:
choices: tapping the underside of a loaf and listening for a hollow sound.
weighing each piece on the scale against the numbers being called out.
pressing a finger into a loaf and watching how the dent filled back in.
timing how long the loaves had sat in the cool cabinet against a clock.
correct_answer: pressing a finger into a loaf and watching how the dent filled back in.
explanation: Paragraph 5 says the father "checked it by pressing one finger into a loaf and watching how the dent came back," and explains that a dent which comes back fast means not ready and one that does not come back means too late. No tapping or listening is described anywhere. The scale belongs to the mother, who uses it to cut the dough into pieces, not to test readiness. The loaves do rest in the retarder "for hours," but no clock or timing is mentioned; the finger test is how readiness is judged.

passage_title: When a River Moves: Two Views
passage:
Passage A

[1] Rivers look permanent on maps, but over long spans of time many of the large ones are restless. A river that carries a heavy load of sand and silt drops some of that load whenever it slows, and much of it settles on the riverbed and along the banks, where floods leave natural ridges called levees. Year by year, the channel and its banks build upward. Eventually the river can be flowing along the top of a low ridge of its own making, higher than the plain on either side.

[2] At that point the river is, in a sense, waiting. Water runs downhill by the steepest route available, and a channel perched above its floodplain offers a longer and gentler route to the sea than the land beside it does. When a large flood breaks through the bank, the water may find that the new path is so much steeper that it never returns. Geologists call this sudden abandonment of one channel for another an avulsion, and it is different from the slow, sideways wandering of a meandering stream. A meander drifts; an avulsion jumps.

[3] The jumps can be enormous. The lower Mississippi has shifted its course several times over the last several thousand years, building a new lobe of its delta each time, and geologists commonly estimate that such a shift has come roughly once every thousand years. China's Yellow River, which carries one of the heaviest sediment loads of any large river, has changed course many times in recorded history; in 1855 it moved its mouth from the south side of the Shandong Peninsula to the north, a shift of hundreds of kilometers.

[4] Human efforts to hold a river in place tend to sharpen the problem they are meant to solve. Artificial levees keep floods off the farms and towns beside the river, but they also keep sediment inside the channel, so the bed keeps rising and the levees must rise with it. Along parts of the lower Yellow River the bed now sits several meters above the surrounding land. Every gain in height makes the eventual break more dangerous. Holding a river, in other words, does not cancel the jump. It postpones it and raises the stakes.

Passage B

[5] Whether a river will move is a question for geologists. What a town does about it is not, and the two questions are too often confused. The physical facts set limits, but within those limits the choices are social: who pays, who moves, and who decides.

[6] Consider two responses to the same kind of threat. After the great Mississippi flood of 1993, the people of Valmeyer, Illinois, a village on the river's floodplain, chose to rebuild their town on the bluffs above the valley rather than behind a stronger levee. The decision was possible partly because the village was small and the higher ground was close. In the Netherlands, where a large share of the land lies below sea level or below the height its rivers reach in flood, abandoning the floodplain was not an option. Beginning in the 2000s, the Dutch government instead moved some dikes back, lowered floodplains, and dug side channels at dozens of sites, deliberately giving rivers more space to spread during high water.

[7] Neither village nor nation was defying geology, and neither was surrendering to it. Valmeyer chose to step aside; the Dutch chose to share. Both choices required years of argument, compensation for those who lost land, and a willingness to accept that the old arrangement could not simply be defended forever.

[8] Where a river threatens a great city, the arithmetic changes again. No one proposes moving New Orleans to higher ground, and the structures that keep the Mississippi from shifting into the channel of the Atchafalaya River will be defended for as long as the money and engineering allow. That is not a failure of imagination. It is a judgment about what is worth protecting, and it belongs to the people who must live with the result.

passage:
[1] For most of the twentieth century, nearly every word on an American main street had been painted by hand. The name on the bakery window, the prices on the grocer's board, the faded advertisement for flour three stories up the side of a brick wall: someone had stood on a plank or a ladder and made each letter with a brush. The people who did this work were called sign painters, or letterers, and they were so common that few passersby ever thought about them at all.

[2] Then, within roughly a decade, the trade nearly disappeared. Beginning in the 1980s, shops could order lettering cut by computer from adhesive vinyl, and the vinyl was cheaper, faster, and, to most eyes, cleaner. A painter who once needed a full day for a storefront could be underbid by a machine that needed an hour. Many letterers retired; others learned the machines. The brushes went into drawers.

[3] I learned the trade late and partly by accident, from a painter named Ida Marsh who had kept working through those years mostly on gold leaf, the one job the machines imitated least convincingly. Ida's shop was a narrow room that smelled of turpentine and coffee. The first thing she gave me was not a brush but a mahl stick, a slender rod with a padded knob at one end. You hold it in your free hand, rest the knob against the glass or the wall, and lay your painting wrist across it, so that your hand floats just above the surface without touching wet paint. "Everything you do," Ida said, "you do from here." It took me a month to stop gripping it as if it might escape.

[4] What I had expected to learn was neatness. What Ida actually taught was decision. A lettering brush holds a long reservoir of paint, and a good stroke is made in one pass, down, turn, lift, because a stroke that is gone over twice shows its seams. You cannot hesitate in the middle of a curve. You decide where the letter will go before the brush touches, and then you commit to it. When I asked Ida how to fix a stroke I had botched, she wiped it off with a rag. "You don't fix it," she said. "You do it again, and this time you mean it."

[5] People who see hand lettering beside vinyl often say the painted version looks warmer, and they usually mean that it is less perfect. That is true as far as it goes, but I think it misses what they are responding to. Vinyl letters are identical because they were never decided; they were selected from a menu. A painted letter carries small traces of a person thinking: an R whose leg kicks out a little farther on the final word because the painter saw that the line needed weight on the right, a gap narrowed where two round letters meet. The irregularity is not decoration. It is the record of a judgment.

[6] In the last fifteen years or so, a modest revival has brought younger painters into the trade, and some shops that could easily afford vinyl now pay more for brushwork. Some of this is fashion, and fashion passes. But Ida, who lived to see the start of it, was less interested in whether the work was popular than in whether it was good. She would walk past a newly painted window and say only, "He looked at it," or, more often, "He didn't look at it," and I understood that she was talking about the whole sign and not any single letter.

[7] I keep her mahl stick in a can on my bench, the knob worn flat on one side from years of resting against glass. I use my own now; hers is too long for my reach. But on difficult jobs I sometimes take it out and hold it for a moment before I begin, the way you might touch a doorframe on your way out of a house. It does not steady my hand. It reminds me what my hand is for.

[1] On certain nights in late spring, in a few forested valleys of the southern Appalachians, thousands of fireflies seem to share a single switch. The males of one species, Photinus carolinus, flash in bursts of several quick pulses, go dark together for several seconds, and then flash again, so that a whole hillside brightens and darkens like a slow breath. In parts of Southeast Asia, males of other species gather by the thousands in mangrove trees along rivers and blink in near-unison for hours. For a long time, many Western scientists who heard such reports doubted them. A firefly, they reasoned, has a tiny brain and no conductor to follow. How could a crowd of them keep time?

[2] The answer that emerged over the following decades is that no conductor is needed. Each male firefly appears to carry an internal timer that sets the rhythm of its flashing, much as a pendulum clock has its own beat. The comparison has limits, since a living timer drifts, but it captures the essential point. On its own, a firefly flashes according to that timer. But the timer can be nudged. In laboratory experiments, researchers flashed an artificial light at individual fireflies and found that a flash seen at the right moment could make an insect flash sooner than it otherwise would have, or later, depending on when in its cycle the light arrived. Each firefly, in effect, adjusts its clock a little toward the flashes it sees.

[3] Mathematicians recognized this arrangement. A population of oscillators, things that repeat a cycle, can fall into step if each one shifts its timing slightly in response to the others, even when no single oscillator is in charge and even when each responds only to its nearest neighbors. Models of such "coupled oscillators" show that synchrony can arise from purely local rules, starting from a crowd in which every member begins at a different point in its cycle. Similar mathematics has since been applied to the pacemaker cells of the heart, which must fire together, and to the chirping of some crickets.

[4] Field studies of Photinus carolinus have added a twist. When researchers placed individual males alone in a tent, the insects flashed at irregular intervals, without the steady rhythm of the swarm. Only when enough males could see one another did the regular bursts appear. If these findings hold, the rhythm is not simply a stored timer that each insect brings to the hillside; it is at least partly a property of the group, something that emerges only when individuals interact. Recordings of whole swarms have also suggested that a burst can begin in one patch of forest and spread outward across it, as if the signal were being passed along.

[5] Why synchronize at all? The flashes are courtship signals: males fly and flash, and females, mostly perched low in the vegetation, answer with flashes of their own. One leading hypothesis holds that synchrony makes a male's pattern easier to recognize. In a forest full of males flashing at random, a female would see a confusing scatter of light; when the males flash together, their shared pattern stands out against the dark intervals. In one laboratory study, females of Photinus carolinus responded far more often to a display of synchronized flashes than to the same flashes out of step. Other researchers suspect that synchrony may be partly a by-product of competition, as each male tries to flash just ahead of his rivals and the timing of the crowd tightens as a result. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive.

[6] Most of the world's roughly two thousand firefly species do not synchronize, and for those that do, the displays are fragile. Artificial light from roads and houses can wash out the dark intervals the signal depends on, and the larvae of many species need undisturbed, moist ground to survive. The insects that solved the problem of keeping time without a conductor have no defense against a porch light.
